justice: Spatial resources are heavily allocated to motor vehicles: multiple wide travel lanes dominate the cross-section, while no visible sidewalk space is provided for pedestrians.
The roadside guardrail on the right edge creates a continuous physical barrier that prevents safe, fair access for non-motorized users to the road edge and adjacent areas.
No visible curb ramps, crossings, or pedestrian facilities (e.g., crosswalks, refuge islands) are present, limiting accessibility for people who are not driving.
safety: Clear lane markings (dashed white lines and solid edge lines) support driver guidance and reduce within-carriageway conflicts.
Right-side metal guardrail provides run-off-road protection for vehicles, reducing the severity of roadside departures.

The roadway appears high-speed and access-controlled (highway-like), and the absence of pedestrian crossings/bike facilities increases risk for any non-motorized user who might enter or need to cross.
livability: The environment is auto-oriented with no visible shops, active frontages, or pedestrian-scale amenities, offering limited support for daily street life.
There are no visible public seating/rest areas, plazas, or gathering points; the corridor functions primarily as a traffic conduit rather than a social space.
The adjacent land uses look sparse/low-activity (vegetation strips and scattered buildings set back), providing weak 'eyes on the street' and limited community vitality.
sustainability: The design strongly prioritizes private motor traffic (multi-lane paved highway), which typically encourages higher-carbon travel compared with transit/walking/cycling-supportive streets.
Some planted vegetation exists in the median/left roadside (trimmed shrubs and trees), offering limited ecological benefit but not forming robust green infrastructure.
No visible public transit infrastructure (bus stops, shelters) or cycling infrastructure (protected lanes, bike parking) is present to support mode shift.
aesthetics: The long, open road vista with consistent markings creates a clean, orderly visual structure.
Landscaped elements (median shrubs and roadside greenery) add some visual softness to an otherwise hardscape-dominated scene.
Utility poles/lines and extensive asphalt surface reduce scenic quality and make the view feel infrastructural rather than place-oriented.
comfort: Thermal comfort is limited: sparse tree canopy and minimal shade along the road edge provide little protection from sun/heat for anyone outside a vehicle.
Physical comfort for non-drivers is poor due to the lack of sidewalks or separated shoulders suitable for walking; the edge condition is constrained by a guardrail.
Psychological comfort for walking/cycling is low because the wide, high-speed roadway and open exposure can feel unsafe and stressful outside a vehicle.
walkability: No visible sidewalk or designated pedestrian path is provided along either side, making continuous walking routes effectively absent.
The right roadside guardrail and narrow edge space prevent comfortable, safe walking even as a last-resort shoulder condition.
No crossings, signals, or pedestrian refuge features are visible, severely limiting connectivity for pedestrians across or along the corridor.
bikeability: No bike lane markings or protected cycling space is visible; cyclists would have to mix with high-speed motor traffic.
The road appears to be a multi-lane, high-speed facility, which typically creates strong overtaking risk and discomfort for people cycling.
There is no visible bicycle support infrastructure (e.g., signage for cycling, bike parking, or separated shoulder continuity) to make cycling practical.
